zh: 一、明治覺觀多病者，如經中說：「覺觀多者，教令數息。」今覺觀之病既有三種，息為對治，亦為三意：一、明利心覺觀者，行者坐中明利之心攀緣，念念不住，此應教令數息。何以故？數息之法，繫心在息，息是治亂之良藥也。若能從一至十，中間不忘，必得入定，能破亂想。數息之法，於沈審心中記數，沈審之心能治明利，是以數息能除明利心中覺觀病也。
en: First, clarifying the treatment for one whose ailment is much discursive thought: as the sūtra says, "One with much discursive thought should be taught to count the breath." Since the ailment of discursive thought is itself of three kinds, the breath serves as its antidote in three corresponding senses as well.

First, treating discursive thought within a sharp, lucid mind: the practitioner's sharp mind, while sitting, chases after its object, never remaining still moment to moment — such a person should be taught to count the breath. Why is this? In the method of counting the breath, the mind is fixed upon the breath, and the breath is the fine medicine for treating disorder. If one is able to count from one to ten without forgetting partway through, concentration is bound to be attained, and scattered thought is thereby broken through. The method of counting the breath keeps count within a settled, deliberate mind, and a settled, deliberate mind is able to treat sharp restlessness — hence counting the breath is able to remove the ailment of discursive thought within a sharp, lucid mind.

zh: 二、明治半明半昏覺觀者，病相如前說，今對治之法，應教令隨息。隨息出入，則心常依息。以依息故，息麁心即麁，息細心亦細，細息出入，繼心緣之，能破覺觀。心靜明鑒，知息出入，長短去就，照用分明，能破昏沈，是故說隨為治。若但數息者，即有扶昏之過。若但觀息，亦有浮亂之失，不名善對治也。三、明治昏沈心中覺觀者，覺觀起相如前說，對治之法，應教令觀息，息入時，諦觀此息從何處來，中間何所經遊，入至何處住。口出息亦如是。此法後當廣說。如是求其根源，出無分散，入無積聚，不見定想，明心觀照，心眼即開，破於沈昏。靜心依息，能破散亂，故以觀息對治沈昏覺觀之病。
en: Second, treating discursive thought within a mind half-lucid and half-dull: the mark of this ailment is as described above; here, the antidote method should teach following the breath instead. As the breath is followed, going out and coming in, the mind constantly relies upon the breath. Because the mind relies upon the breath, when the breath is coarse the mind, too, is coarse, and when the breath is fine the mind, too, becomes fine — as the fine breath goes out and comes in, the mind, sustained by following it, is thereby able to break through discursive thought. The mind, stilled and clearly discerning, knows the breath's coming and going, its length and direction, illuminating it distinctly — able thereby to break through dullness and sinking as well. Hence following the breath is said to be its antidote. Were one to use counting the breath alone, there would be the fault of encouraging dullness; were one to use observing the breath alone, there would be the fault of encouraging restlessness — neither, by itself, could be called a properly matched antidote.

Third, treating discursive thought within a mind sunk in dullness: the mark of discursive thought arising here is as described above; the antidote method should teach observing the breath instead. As the breath enters, one closely observes exactly where this breath comes from, what course it travels through in between, and where it finally comes to rest upon entering; the same applies to the breath as it goes out through the mouth — this method will be explained more fully later. Tracing the breath back to its very root source in this way, one finds that, going out, it does not scatter, and, coming in, it does not accumulate; no fixed notion of it can be found at all. The mind grows clear, contemplating and illuminating; the mind's own eye thereby opens, breaking through sunken dullness. A mind stilled through relying on the breath is able to break through scattered disorder — hence observing the breath serves as the antidote to the ailment of discursive thought within sunken dullness.

zh: 二、明治貪欲多病，如經中說：「貪欲多者，教不淨觀。」欲病既有三種，今對治亦為三意：一、明治外貪欲多者，病發從著外境男女容色、姿態、語言、威儀、細滑等相，是故婬火熾然不息。對治之法，應教作九想觀，若至塚間取死屍相，亦當諦觀可愛之境，躃著地上，觀見死屍胮脹、爛壞、膿血流出、大小便利、諸蟲唼食。今我著者亦復如是，何處可愛？作是觀已，婬心自息，是故九想能治愛著外境貪婬重病。
en: Second, clarifying the treatment for one whose ailment is much craving: as the sūtra says, "One with much craving should be taught the contemplation of impurity." Since the ailment of desire is itself of three kinds, its antidote likewise has three corresponding senses.

First, treating one whose ailment is much external craving: this ailment arises from attachment to the form of men and women as external objects — their appearance, manner, speech, bearing, smooth skin, and other such marks, so that the fire of lust burns on without ceasing. The antidote method should teach the practice of the nine contemplations: going, if possible, to a charnel ground to take up the mark of an actual corpse, closely observing this very object once found so lovely, now fallen flat upon the ground, observing the corpse swollen, decaying, pus and blood flowing out, excrement and urine, and the various worms devouring it — reflecting that what I myself am so attached to is exactly the same as this: where, in it, could there possibly be anything to love? Once this contemplation is made, the mind of lust comes to rest of itself — hence the nine contemplations are able to treat the grave ailment of craving attached to an external object.

zh: 二、明治內外貪欲煩惱，煩惱病發如前說，若欲治之，當教作初背捨等觀，諦觀內身不淨，破壞可惡，即破緣內貪愛，復當如前，觀外不淨可惡，即離外境貪愛，即是初背捨，以是不淨心觀內外色，能破內外愛著貪婬之病。三、明治一切處皆起貪愛者，貪病發相，如前說。治法，應教緣一切處大不淨觀，觀一切境男女、自身、他身、田園、屋宅、衣服、飲食、一切世間所有，皆見不淨，無有一處可生貪心，爾時一切處中生厭離心，則一切貪欲無復起處，是名對治一切處貪欲病。
en: Second, treating the affliction of craving both external and internal: the arising of this affliction is as described above. To treat it, one should be taught to practice the first liberation and its related contemplations, closely observing the inner body as impure, decaying, and repugnant, thereby breaking through craving that takes the inward body as its object; and, as before, observing the outward body as impure and repugnant as well, thereby leaving behind craving that takes an external object — this is precisely the first liberation. Through this mind that contemplates form, both inward and outward, as impure, one is able to break through the ailment of craving attached both externally and internally.

Third, treating one in whom craving arises toward every place without exception: the mark of this ailment's arising is as described above. The treatment method should teach the great contemplation of impurity taking every place as its object, observing every state — men and women, one's own body, others' bodies, fields and gardens, houses, clothing, food and drink, everything whatsoever in the world — all seen as impure, with not a single place left where a craving mind could possibly arise; at that point, a mind of weariness and detachment arises with respect to every place, and craving no longer has anywhere left to arise from at all. This is called the antidote to the ailment of craving toward every place.

zh: 三、明治瞋恚多病，如經中說：「瞋恚多者，教慈心觀。」治瞋病既有三種，今對治亦復有三：一、明治邪瞋者，日夜心中思惟非理，欲以惡事惱他瞋發之相，具如上說。治之，應令修眾生緣慈，取一親人得樂之相，緣之入定。如是見親人得樂中，怨人等皆令得樂，取他樂相，能生愛念，即破於眾生中瞋惱怨害之心。
en: Third, clarifying the treatment for one whose ailment is much anger: as the sūtra says, "One with much anger should be taught the contemplation of loving-kindness." Since the ailment of anger is itself of three kinds, its antidote likewise has three corresponding forms.

First, treating deviant anger: day and night, the mind dwells on what is contrary to reason, wishing to trouble another through some unwholesome act — the mark of this ailment's arising is exactly as described above. To treat it, one should be led to cultivate loving-kindness that takes sentient beings as its object, taking up the mark of a single loved one's happiness and taking this as the object through which concentration is entered. Seeing this loved one gaining happiness in this way, one then lets enemies and the like all gain happiness as well — taking up the mark of another's happiness in this way is able to give rise to a loving regard, thereby breaking through the mind of anger, vexation, and enmity harbored toward sentient beings.

zh: 二、明治正瞋者，若於餘事之中都無瞋心，但見人作惡，或復犯戒而起瞋心病發之相，具如前說。治之，應教修法緣慈，觀五陰虛假，不見眾生，豈有持犯是非之事？但緣諸受中法樂，以與於他，慈心愛念，不應加惱。是非既泯，瞋心自息，是為行法緣慈能治順理瞋病。三、明治一切法中諍論故瞋者，病發如前說。對治方法，應教修無緣慈。何以故？此人隨所得法，既自以為是，謂他即非，同我者喜，違我者即瞋，或於四句及絕四句中生執，或復執於中道。如是皆有所依，故有諍訟執計因緣，便生瞋覺。對治方法，令修無緣之慈，行此慈時，言語道斷，心行處滅，於一切法不憶不念。若無憶念，因何諍訟而生瞋心？大慈平等，同與本淨之樂，離惱他相，故名慈能與樂。亦得言菩薩為諸眾生說如是法，名為大慈。當知修無緣慈對治一切法中諍論瞋恚。
en: Second, treating correct anger: this is a person with no angry mind at all in every other matter, yet who, simply upon seeing another do wrong, or violate the precepts, has an angry mind arise — the mark of this ailment's arising is exactly as described above. To treat it, one should be taught to cultivate loving-kindness that takes dharma as its object, contemplating the five aggregates as empty and unreal, so that no sentient being is seen at all — how, then, could there be any matter of upholding or violating, right or wrong, to speak of? One simply takes the dharma-joy present within every sensation and offers it to others, a mind of loving-kindness and affection that ought never to add further vexation. Once right and wrong have dissolved away in this manner, the angry mind comes to rest of itself — hence practicing loving-kindness that takes dharma as its object is able to treat anger in accord with reason.

Third, treating anger through disputation over every dharma: the mark of this ailment's arising is exactly as described above. The antidote method should teach the cultivation of objectless loving-kindness. Why is this? Such a person, whatever teaching they have grasped, takes it to be correct of themselves and takes another's as therefore mistaken — delighting in whoever agrees, growing angry at whoever differs — clinging, perhaps, to one of the four propositions or to their total negation, or even clinging to the middle way itself. In every such case there is something relied upon, and so there is contention and fixed conceptual grasping as its cause and condition, giving rise to an angry thought. The antidote method has one cultivate objectless loving-kindness instead: in practicing this loving-kindness, the path of language is cut off, the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, and with respect to every dharma there is nothing recalled, nothing dwelt upon. If there is nothing recalled or dwelt upon, on what basis could contention give rise to an angry mind at all? Great loving-kindness, equal toward all, bestows this same, originally pure happiness on every being alike, free of any mark of troubling another — hence loving-kindness is said to be that which bestows happiness. It may also be said that when a bodhisattva teaches this same dharma to sentient beings, this, too, is called great loving-kindness. One should know that cultivating objectless loving-kindness serves as the antidote to anger through disputation over every dharma.
